title: Character work
hook: the Musar movement works on one character trait at a time

segments.voice: Yesterday, kavanah: directed intention, the heart aimed at what the hands or lips are doing. Your line was kavanah. Which small act did you aim, and how did it go? Day one thousand three hundred eighty-three.

Ask a friend what kind of person they'd like to become, and the list can come fast. More patient. More generous. Honest even when it costs something. Calmer in traffic. Kinder to their brother. Ask when they're starting, and the list goes quiet. Where would anyone begin with all that? A Jewish movement of teachers gave an answer so plain it can sound like a trick. Don't start with the list. Start with one line on it, and stay there a while. Today's word is the name of that movement.
screen: `A LIST OF WHO YOU'D LIKE TO BE.` → `WHERE WOULD ANYONE BEGIN?` → `ONE LINE ON THE LIST.`

segments.voice: The word is Musar. In the book of Proverbs, musar is a Hebrew word for instruction or correction. The King James Bible gives the line this way: "My son, hear the instruction of thy father, and forsake not the law of thy mother." Jewish teachers used the word for writing about character, and a rabbi named Israel Salanter made it the name of a movement. Its starting point is simple. The traits of a person, in Hebrew middot, can be worked on like a skill. Not admired from far off. Practiced. Patience, order, humility, generosity, honesty, calm. And the Musar way takes them one at a time. A saying often attributed to Salanter puts the difficulty bluntly: it is easier to learn the whole Talmud than to change a single trait. So you don't try to change them all. You pick one. You watch it through the day, noticing where it holds and where it slips. Some practitioners write a line about it each night. Some repeat a short phrase about it, often a line from a text, until it settles in. After a stretch, they move to the next trait. The movement stood on older Jewish wisdom about strength. The Mishnah's Ethics of the Fathers asks who is mighty, and answers with a verse from Proverbs: "He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city." Ruling your own spirit, in that line, counts for more than taking a city. Musar treats that inner work as the hard part, and the small daily gain as the real one. Not a new self by Friday. A little more patience by the end of the month.
screen: `MUSAR: INSTRUCTION, CORRECTION.` · `TRAITS CAN BE PRACTICED.` · `ONE TRAIT AT A TIME.` · `RULING YOUR OWN SPIRIT.` · then, large: `HE THAT RULETH HIS SPIRIT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pick one trait to work on. Sit, and let the breath settle. Let a short list pass slowly through your mind: patience, honesty, generosity, order, humility, calm. Don't choose the one you think you ought to. Choose the one where yesterday went wrong. When did you snap, rush, hold back, or cover something over? Name that trait in one plain word. If you pray, you can ask for help with it. If you don't, simply hold the word, and let it sit with you. The bell holds the time.
Musar. Instruction, correction: a Jewish movement of character work, practicing one trait at a time. Today's word.
Your line: one trait. Today, keep the trait you chose close by. Notice one moment where it shows up, and tonight write a single line about how it went. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-three.

howItsDone: People who practice Musar often choose one middah, a trait such as patience or humility, and attend to it for a period of time, with daily notes, study of Musar texts and short repeated phrases, sometimes in a small group.

what it means: a Jewish practice of character work, taking one trait at a time and working on it daily.
what a scholar hears: the Proverbs word for instruction, taken up as the name of Israel Salanter's movement, with the middot worked one by one.

notes: Confirm that the Hebrew word rendered 'instruction' in Proverbs 1:8 is musar (מוּסַר).
Index hook's '19th century' left out under the claims rule; the script gives no date or place for Salanter.
The saying 'it is easier to learn the whole Talmud than to change one trait' is widely attributed to Salanter but its source is uncertain; it is presented as 'often attributed'. Confirm or cut.

Musar practices described (one trait for a period, nightly notes, repeated phrases from a text, groups) are stated as what 'some practitioners' do; confirm they fairly describe historical and contemporary Musar.
